title: Consider your ways (Haggai 1:2–8)
hook: you eat but aren't full; you earn wages into a bag with holes

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dies Irae, and the surprise at the end of Zephaniah: God sings over you. Your line: sung over.

Payday. The money lands, and by the end of the week, somehow, it's gone. Not on anything big. Just leaking: groceries that didn't last, subscriptions you forgot, little fixes on things that keep breaking. Working hard and never quite getting ahead. An old prophet named Haggai described exactly that, with an image anyone who's carried coins can picture: a bag with holes in it. He wasn't talking to lazy people. He was talking to people who were busy, and tired, and couldn't figure out why it never felt like enough.

Haggai's first message is dated to the day: the second year of King Darius, the sixth month, the first day. The exiles have come home from Babylon to Jerusalem, and the temple is still a ruin. People say it isn't the right time to rebuild. Haggai's answer, in the King James Bible: "Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?" Cieled means paneled, finished nicely, while God's house sits in rubble. Then: "Consider your ways." In Hebrew it's more vivid: set your heart on your ways. Look hard at where your life is going. Then the list: "Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes." Every line has the same shape: effort in, nothing to show for it. Haggai's diagnosis is that the people have put their own houses first and left the center empty. So the cure is surprisingly practical: go up to the mountain, bring wood, and build. Christians read Haggai more than one way. Some hear it about church buildings and giving. Others hear it more broadly: when the most important thing in a life is left in ruins, everything else leaks. And the people listened. Before the month was out, by Haggai's own dates, they started rebuilding.
screen: `DATED TO THE DAY: A TEMPLE IN RUINS.`

segments.voice: Picture your last week as a bag you've been filling with time, energy, money and attention, and find one hole: hours on a screen that left you emptier, or worry about something you can't change. Then ask Haggai's question: what's the thing at the center I've left in ruins? If you pray, set it before God and ask for one first step; if not, simply name it, and name the first piece of wood.
Cieled. The old word for paneled, finished nicely: the houses Haggai says the people built for themselves while God's house lay in ruins.
Your line: a bag with holes. The people listened, and started to build. Day four hundred ninety-three, done.

howItsDone: Some churches read Haggai when they are building or rebuilding, and some Christians use its call to consider your ways as a prompt for an honest review of how they spend their time and money.

A warning that thieves were stealing the temple's money from the priests.

Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes.

notes: Haggai 1:1 is dated to the first day of the sixth month of Darius's second year, generally 520 BC (late August). Confirm.
Haggai 1:15 dates the start of work to the 24th day of the same month: 'within weeks'. Confirm.
'Set your heart on your ways' as the literal Hebrew (simu levavchem al darcheichem). Confirm.
Two Christian readings (church buildings and giving; ordering life around what matters most) given without ranking.

Editor pass (y2 review): the BC conversions ('520 BC', 'twenty-five centuries ago') are not in the text, so the lesson now gives Haggai's own date (Darius's second year, sixth month, first day, 1:1) and 'before the month was out' (1:15, the 24th day). The hook's 'purse with a hole' now matches the KJV 'bag with holes'; 'one of the few prophets', 'years after their return', stock 'good news hiding in the book', 'often/many' claims, and the hook telling the listener their situation were fixed.
